notes.text: **Genesis 27:4** — וַעֲשֵׂה לִי מַטְעַמִּים כַּאֲשֶׁר אָהַבְתִּי... בַּעֲבוּר תְּבָרֶכְךָ נַפְשִׁי בְּטֶרֶם אָמוּת — Isaac asks Esau for a dish he loves, so that his soul may bless him “before I die.” The whole os turns on why Isaac adds “before I die” here. *Mafteach: found*

**Genesis 27:2** — הִנֵּה נָא זָקַנְתִּי לֹא יָדַעְתִּי יוֹם מוֹתִי — “I have grown old; I do not know the day of my death.” Since Isaac has already said he does not know when he will die, Rav Tzadok treats the later “before I die” as extra words that need explaining. *Mafteach: missing*

**Rashi on Genesis 27:2** (after R. Yehoshua ben Korchah) — אִם מַגִּיעַ אָדָם לְפֶרֶק אֲבוֹתָיו יִדְאַג חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים לִפְנֵיהֶן... וְיִצְחָק הָיָה בֶּן קכ"ג, אָמַר שֶׁמָּא לְפֶרֶק אִמִּי אֲנִי מַגִּיעַ — someone nearing the age at which a parent died should worry for five years before it. Isaac was 123 and Sarah died at 127, so he feared he had reached her age. The fifty-seven further years in [1.7] come from this: 123 now, and 180 at his death (Genesis 35:28). *Mafteach: missing*

**Genesis 27:7** — הָבִיאָה לִּי צַיִד וַעֲשֵׂה לִי מַטְעַמִּים וְאֹכֵלָה וַאֲבָרֶכְכָה לִפְנֵי ה' לִפְנֵי מוֹתִי — Rebecca, quoting Isaac to Jacob, adds “before Hashem” next to “before my death.” In [6.7] Rav Tzadok reads the two phrases together. *Mafteach: missing*
**Genesis 27:10** — וְהֵבֵאתָ לְאָבִיךָ וְאָכָל בַּעֲבֻר אֲשֶׁר יְבָרֶכְךָ לִפְנֵי מוֹתוֹ — Rebecca says “before his death” a second time, now in her own words to Jacob. *Mafteach: missing*

**Deuteronomy 33:1** — וְזֹאת הַבְּרָכָה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרַךְ מֹשֶׁה אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לִפְנֵי מוֹתוֹ — the blessing Moses gave Israel “before his death.” For Rav Tzadok this is the plain use of the phrase: the blessing came right before the death itself. *Mafteach: found*

**The tradition that Moses passed away on Shabbat, at the time of Minchah** — *Sefer HaOrah* I 59: לְפִי שֶׁמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ מֵת בְּמִנְחָה בְּשַׁבָּת; the Bach (Tur OC 292) gives it in the Zohar's name (Terumah): וּבְמִנְחָה בְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁאָז הוּא עֵת רָצוֹן אִסְתַּלַּק מֵעָלְמָא. This tradition is the reason Tzidkascha is said at Shabbat Minchah. Rav Tzadok uses it to show that Moses' blessing came on the very day he died. *Mafteach: missing*

**Midrash Tanchuma, Toldot 1** — גָּדוֹל הוּא הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁדִּבְּרָה הַתּוֹרָה דִּבְרֵי בְדַאי בִּשְׁבִיל שָׁלוֹם. וְאֵי זֶה, כֹּה תֹאמְרוּ לְיוֹסֵף... וְאֵין אָנוּ מוֹצְאִים שֶׁצִּוָּה כְּלוּם מִכָּל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה — peace is so great that the Torah records invented words for its sake: Jacob never gave the command the brothers attributed to him. Rav Tzadok's question follows from this: the Torah records something untrue only for a reason, so what is the reason for Isaac's “before I die”? *Mafteach: found*

**Genesis 50:16–17** — אָבִיךָ צִוָּה לִפְנֵי מוֹתוֹ לֵאמֹר. כֹּה תֹאמְרוּ לְיוֹסֵף אָנָּא שָׂא נָא פֶּשַׁע אַחֶיךָ — the brothers' message to Joseph that their father had commanded “before his death.” The same phrase, לִפְנֵי מוֹתוֹ, appears here in a statement that was not literally true. *Mafteach: wrong label (index: שמות סט)*

**Shabbat 153a** (citing Avot 2:10) — רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: שׁוּב יוֹם אֶחָד לִפְנֵי מִיתָתֶךָ... יָשׁוּב הַיּוֹם שֶׁמָּא יָמוּת לְמָחָר, וְנִמְצָא כׇּל יָמָיו בִּתְשׁוּבָה — repent a day before you die; since no one knows that day, repent today, and all your days are spent in repentance. Rav Tzadok asks why it says “one day before your death” instead of simply “lest you die tomorrow.” *Mafteach: found*

**Exodus 20:9** — שֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים תַּעֲבֹד וְעָשִׂיתָ כׇּל מְלַאכְתֶּךָ — “Six days you shall labor and do all your work.” This is the verse the Mekhilta expounds (the same words appear in Deuteronomy 5:13). *Mafteach: found*

**Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael, Bachodesh 7** (on Exodus 20:9) — וְכִי אֶפְשָׁר לְבָשָׂר וָדָם לַעֲשׂוֹת כָּל מְלַאכְתּוֹ בְּשֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים? אֶלָּא שְׁבֹת כְּאִלּוּ כָּל מְלַאכְתָּךְ עֲשׂוּיָה. דָּבָר אַחֵר: שְׁבֹת מִמַּחְשֶׁבֶת עֲבוֹדָה — no one finishes all his work in six days, so rest as though it were all finished; or, rest even from thinking about work. Rav Tzadok explains the first reading through the Zohar ([3.13]) and the second through the Tur ([3.6]). *Mafteach: found*

**Tur, Orach Chaim 306** (end) — וְהִרְהוּר בַּעֲסָקָיו מוּתָּר, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מִשּׁוּם עֹנֶג שַׁבָּת מִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא יַחְשׁוֹב בָּהֶם כְּלָל... אֶלָּא יִרְאֶה אָדָם בְּכָל שַׁבָּת כְּאִילּוּ מְלַאכְתּוֹ עֲשׂוּיָה — thinking about one's business is permitted, but delight in Shabbat calls for not thinking about it at all, as though one's work were done. *Mafteach: missing*

**Zohar II 205a** (Vayakhel) — הַאי יוֹמָא, יוֹמָא דְּנִשְׁמָתִין אִיהוּ, וְלָאו יוֹמָא דְּגוּפָא, בְּגִין דְּשֻׁלְטָנוּ דִּצְרוֹרָא דְּנִשְׁמָתִין אִיהוּ — Shabbat is a day of souls, not of the body, because then the place where souls are bound up is in charge. Rav Tzadok uses this to explain “as though your work were done”: on a day of souls, bodily work has nothing left to claim. *Mafteach: found*

**Ecclesiastes 9:8**, quoted at **Shabbat 153a** right after R. Eliezer's teaching — וְאַף שְׁלֹמֹה אָמַר בְּחָכְמָתוֹ: בְּכׇל עֵת יִהְיוּ בְגָדֶיךָ לְבָנִים וְשֶׁמֶן עַל רֹאשְׁךָ אַל יֶחְסָר — “at all times let your garments be white, and let your head never lack oil.” The Gemara follows it with R. Yochanan ben Zakkai's parable of the king who invited his servants to a feast without setting a time. *Mafteach: found*

**Job 10:11** — עוֹר וּבָשָׂר תַּלְבִּישֵׁנִי וּבַעֲצָמוֹת וְגִידִים תְּשֹׂכְכֵנִי — “You clothed me in skin and flesh, and wove me with bones and sinews.” The verb “clothed” is what lets Rav Tzadok read “your garments” as the body. *Mafteach: wrong address (index: Job 5:11; correct: Job 10:11)*

**Zohar II 75b–76a** (Yitro) — עוֹר וּבָשָׂר תַּלְבִּישֵׁנִי... אִי הָכִי הָאָדָם מַהוּ... הָאָדָם לָאו אִיהוּ אֶלָּא נִשְׁמְתָא, וְאִלֵּין... כֻּלְּהוּ לָא הֲווֹ אֶלָּא מַלְבּוּשָׁא — the person is only the soul; skin, flesh, bones and sinews are its clothing, tools of the person and not the person. The wording “flesh of man” (בְּשַׂר אָדָם) is spelled out in **Zohar I 20b**: וּבְכָל אֲתַר כְּתִיב בְּשַׂר אָדָם, אָדָם לְגוֹ, בָּשָׂר לְבוּשָׁא דְּאָדָם. *Mafteach: wrong address (index: Zohar I 8b; correct: Zohar II 76a)*

**Isaiah 1:18** — אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ — “if your sins are like scarlet, they will turn white as snow.” Here white stands for deeds that have been purified. *Mafteach: found*
**Psalms 51:9** — תְּחַטְּאֵנִי בְאֵזוֹב וְאֶטְהָר תְּכַבְּסֵנִי וּמִשֶּׁלֶג אַלְבִּין — “Purge me with hyssop and I will be pure; wash me and I will be whiter than snow.” *Mafteach: found*

**Menachot 85b** — וַיִּשְׁלַח יוֹאָב תְּקוֹעָה וַיִּקַּח מִשָּׁם אִשָּׁה חֲכָמָה... מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁרְגִילִין בְּשֶׁמֶן זַיִת, חָכְמָה מְצוּיָה בָּהֶן — the people of Tekoa were known for wisdom because they used olive oil regularly. This is the source for oil standing for wisdom, which lets Rav Tzadok read “oil on your head” as the repair of thought. *Mafteach: found*

**Shabbat 153a** — דָּבָר אַחֵר: בְּכׇל עֵת יִהְיוּ בְגָדֶיךָ לְבָנִים — אֵלּוּ צִיצִית, וְשֶׁמֶן עַל רֹאשְׁךָ אַל יֶחְסָר — אֵלּוּ תְּפִילִּין — the Gemara's second reading of the verse: white garments are tzitzit, oil on the head is tefillin. Rav Tzadok sets these against action and thought. *Mafteach: found*
**Nedarim 25a** — שְׁקוּלָה מִצְוַת צִיצִית כְּנֶגֶד כׇּל מִצְוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה — the mitzvah of tzitzit is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah. *Mafteach: found*

**Numbers 15:40** — לְמַעַן תִּזְכְּרוּ וַעֲשִׂיתֶם אֶת כׇּל מִצְוֹתָי וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים לֵאלֹהֵיכֶם — the tzitzit passage connects the fringes with doing “all My commandments.” Rav Tzadok links “and do” to the positive commandments, which come from love. *Mafteach: found*

**Zohar, Terumah** (Sefaria, Terumah 44:482) — אוּף הָכִי תְּכֵלֶת וּרְאִיתֶם אוֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם אֶת כָּל מִצְוֹת ה', מֵהַהוּא דְּחִילוּ דִּילֵיהּ — like the copper serpent, techelet brings a person to awe of God. Also **Zohar, Shelach** (Sefaria, Sh'lach 46:328): בְּגִין דִּתְכֵלֶת... וְדָא אִיהוּ דַּחֲלָא מִן קֳדָם ה' — techelet stands for fear. The Mafteach files these under Zohar II 149b and III 159a; I have not checked those page numbers against a printed edition. *Mafteach: found*

**Peri Tzadik, Chayei Sarah 7** — שֶׁמִּדָּתוֹ הָיָה אַהֲבָה... שֶׁשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַמִּצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה בָּא עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. וּמִדַּת יִצְחָק הַפַּחַד וְהַיִּרְאָה וּמִזֶּה בָּא הַשְּׁמִירָה בְּמִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה — Abraham's trait, love, is the root of the positive commandments. Isaac's trait, fear, is the root of guarding the negative ones. Rav Tzadok cites the Yerushalmi there (Berachos 9, quoted in Tosafot, Sotah 22b). *Mafteach: missing*

**Zechariah 3:3–4** — וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ הָיָה לָבֻשׁ בְּגָדִים צוֹאִים... הָסִירוּ הַבְּגָדִים הַצֹּאִים מֵעָלָיו... רְאֵה הֶעֱבַרְתִּי מֵעָלֶיךָ עֲוֺנֶךָ — Joshua the High Priest stands in filthy garments, and removing them is explained as removing his sin. This shows that a person's deeds become his clothing. *Mafteach: found*

**The meditation said before putting on tefillin** (printed in the siddur; quoted in Olat Re'iyah, Tefillin 7) — וְעַל הָרֹאשׁ כְּנֶגֶד הַמּוֹחַ, שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה שֶׁבְּמוֹחִי עִם שְׁאָר חוּשַׁי וְכֹחוֹתַי כֻּלָּם יִהְיוּ מְשׁוּעְבָּדִים לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ — the head tefillin are placed against the brain so that the mind and all one's senses and faculties are given over to His service. Rav Tzadok quotes it from memory, with “thought” in place of “soul.” *Mafteach: missing*

**Zohar I 141a** (Toldot) — וְכֵן אַבְרָהָם אִשְׁתַּדַּל וְחָפַר בֵּירָא דְמַיָא, יַעֲקֹב אַשְׁכַּח לֵיהּ מִתְתַּקַּן וְיָתִיב עֲלֵיהּ... בְּגִין לְאִתְתַּקְפָא בִּמְהֵימְנוּתָא שְׁלֵימָתָא — Abraham and Isaac dug wells to strengthen themselves in complete faith, and Jacob found the well already in place and settled by it. The Zohar goes on: וְהַשְׁתָּא יִשְׂרָאֵל אִתְתַּקָּפוּ בֵּיהּ בְּרָזֵי דְּפִקּוּדֵי אוֹרַיְיתָא... בְּצִיצִית... הָכִי נָמֵי בִּתְפִלֵּי דְּמַנַּח אֲרֵישֵׁיהּ וּבִדְרוֹעֵיהּ (quoted in [8.12]–[8.13]). *Mafteach: found*

**Taanit 5b** — אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ לֹא מֵת... מַקִּישׁ הוּא לְזַרְעוֹ: מָה זַרְעוֹ בַּחַיִּים — אַף הוּא בַּחַיִּים — “Jacob our father did not die”; the verse compares him to his descendants, and as they are alive, so is he. Rav Tzadok explains this as Jacob being like Adam before the sin, with no waste (pesoles) coming out of him. *Mafteach: missing*

**Genesis 3:1** — וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל הָאִשָּׁה אַף כִּי אָמַר אֱלֹהִים לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן — the serpent's opening question. Rav Tzadok reads it as: even if God commanded, you are not bound to obey. *Mafteach: found*

**Genesis 3:5** — כִּי יֹדֵעַ אֱלֹהִים כִּי בְּיוֹם אֲכׇלְכֶם מִמֶּנּוּ וְנִפְקְחוּ עֵינֵיכֶם וִהְיִיתֶם כֵּאלֹהִים יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע — “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” *Mafteach: found*

**Bereshit Rabbah 19:4** — אָמַר מֵאִילָן הַזֶּה אָכַל וּבָרָא הָעוֹלָם, וְהוּא אוֹמֵר לָכֶם לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ, שֶׁלֹּא תִבְרְאוּ עוֹלָמוֹת אֲחֵרִים — the serpent claimed that God ate from this tree and created the world, and forbade it so that they would not create other worlds. Rav Tzadok calls this heresy: denying God's absolute divinity. *Mafteach: missing*

**Rashi on Genesis 24:7** (on Genesis 24:3, וּאֱלֹהֵי הָאָרֶץ) — עַכְשָׁו הוּא אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וֵאלֹהֵי הָאָרֶץ, שֶׁהִרְגַּלְתִּיו בְּפִי הַבְּרִיּוֹת — Abraham says God is now also “God of the earth,” because Abraham made His name familiar to people. *Mafteach: missing*

**Genesis 18:27** — הִנֵּה נָא הוֹאַלְתִּי לְדַבֵּר אֶל אֲדֹנָי וְאָנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵפֶר — “I am but dust and ashes.” Abraham's humility answers the serpent's “you will be like God.” *Mafteach: missing*

**Genesis 18:19** — לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו וְאֶת בֵּיתוֹ אַחֲרָיו וְשָׁמְרוּ דֶּרֶךְ ה' לַעֲשׂוֹת צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט — Abraham commands his household to keep the way of Hashem. This answers the serpent's claim that one need not obey. *Mafteach: missing*

**Genesis 22** (the Akeidah) and **Avot 5:3** — עֲשָׂרָה נִסְיוֹנוֹת נִתְנַסָּה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְעָמַד בְּכֻלָּם — Abraham was tested ten times and passed them all; Rav Tzadok counts the binding of Isaac as the tenth, as Peri Tzadik does elsewhere (cf. Chayei Sarah 7, citing Tanchuma Vayera). *Mafteach: missing*

**Genesis 24:62** — וְיִצְחָק בָּא מִבּוֹא בְּאֵר לַחַי רֹאִי וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב — Isaac “dwelt in the land of the Negev.” Through the Gemara's reading of נֶגֶב as “dried out” (Temurah 16a: בַּיִת שֶׁמְּנוּגָּב מִכׇּל טוֹבָה), Rav Tzadok takes this to mean Isaac was drained of every craving. *Mafteach: found*

**Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 1** — עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁדָּרְשׁוּ (תְּמוּרָה טז.) כִּי אֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב נְתַתָּנִי בַּיִת שֶׁמְּנוּגָּב מִכָּל טוֹבָה... וּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ נַיְיחָא בְּמִדָּה זוֹ שֶׁהָיָה מְבוֹרָר בְּמִדַּת הַצִּמְצוּם הַפַּחַד וְהַיִּרְאָה — Abraham journeyed toward the Negev, and Isaac dwelt there settled, refined in the trait of restraint and fear. *Mafteach: missing*

**The Arizal's Shabbat-morning song** (אֲסַדֵּר לִסְעוּדָתָא בְּצַפְרָא דְשַׁבַּתָּא) — נְהוֹרֵיהּ יִשְׁרֵי בָהּ, בְּקִדּוּשָׁא רַבָּא, וּבְחַמְרָא טָבָא — “may His light rest upon it, with the great Kiddush and with good wine,” sung at the daytime meal (סְעוּדָתָא דְּעַתִּיקָא). Rav Tzadok takes “His light” to be the light of the first day. *Mafteach: missing*

**Genesis 1:3** — וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי אוֹר — the first utterance of creation. Rav Tzadok reads it as the revelation of Chochmah, the “brain” among the sefirot, which links the morning meal to repairing thought. *Mafteach: missing*

**A tradition about R. Elimelech of Lizhensk**, told in his son's name: that “all his days he commanded ‘before his death.’” I could not find this saying in the printed sources I searched, including Sefaria's Chassidic library. It appears to be an oral tradition Rav Tzadok received. *Mafteach: missing*

**Parallels:** **Peri Tzadik, Vayeshev 8** (Rav Tzadok) — the same Tanchuma (“the Torah recorded invented words for the sake of peace”) and the same principle: the Written Torah would not record something untrue without a lesson. Here it is used for Jacob's “a wild beast has devoured him.” It adds that what a tzaddik says comes true at a deeper level, which matches the way this os turns Isaac's “before I die” into something true. *checked*

**Parallels:** **Peri Tzadik, Matot 6** (Rav Tzadok) — the same pairing of Zohar II 205a (“a day of souls”) with the Mekhilta: “immediately as Shabbat begins, all his bodily work is done and finished.” It adds that Isaac, whose soul left him at the Akeidah, lived all his days “like a day of souls,” which is why the Friday-night meal is his. *checked*
**Peri Tzadik, Vayigash 6** (Rav Tzadok) — the same Zohar, with a second line from it: וּבְכָל מַעֲלֵי שַׁבְּתָא יָתִיב בַּר נָשׁ בְּעוֹלַם הַנְּשָׁמוֹת (every Shabbat eve a person sits in the world of souls). It reads R. Chanina's “come, let us go out to greet Shabbat” as going out of bodily concerns. *checked*

**Parallels:** **Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 4** (Rav Tzadok) — the same reading of Isaac: וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב מְנוּגָּב מִכָּל תַּאֲוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה. Like this os, it has Abraham and Isaac digging wells while Jacob “found wells already dug,” and Jacob “did not die” because his offspring had no waste. *checked*

**Parallels:** **Peri Tzadik, Balak 12** (Rav Tzadok) — gives the source of this order: הָאֲרִ"י הַקָּדוֹשׁ סִידֵּר הַסְּעוּדוֹת דְּשַׁבָּת בַּלַּיְלָה נֶגֶד יִצְחָק... וּבַבֹּקֶר כְּנֶגֶד אַבְרָהָם... וּסְעוּדָה ג' כְּנֶגֶד יַעֲקֹב. It adds that Jacob's meal includes all three patriarchs, because only from Jacob was there no waste. *checked*
**Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 4** (Rav Tzadok) — the morning meal is Abraham's (סְעוּדָתָא דְּעַתִּיקָא) and the night meal is Isaac's (חֲקַל תַּפּוּחִין), the field Isaac smelled on Jacob. It connects the night meal to repairing Adam's sin, as this os does with Isaac and the repair of action. *checked*

**Parallels beyond the library:** **Be'er Mayim Chaim, Genesis 27:3** (Chassidus) — R. Chaim of Czernowitz also ties Isaac's “I do not know the day of my death” to R. Eliezer's “repent one day before your death.” In his reading Isaac is urging Esau to repent today. Rav Tzadok instead turns it on Isaac himself, standing as if at death.
כִּי אָמַר לוֹ הֲרֵי לֹא יָדַעְתִּי יוֹם מוֹתִי... וְעַל כֵּן רָאוּי שֶׁתָּשׁוּב תֵּיכֶף בַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה כְּאוֹמְרָם ז"ל שׁוּב יוֹם אֶחָד לִפְנֵי מִיתָתְךָ

**Parallels beyond the library:** **Shelah, Torah Shebikhtav, Vayakhel–Pekudei, Torah Ohr 28** (Musar/Kabbalah) — reads the Mekhilta as the hidden side of “guarding” Shabbat in the body: besides not working, one should feel when Shabbat arrives that all one's work is finished.
יִהְיֶה בְּעֵינָיו בְּבוֹא שַׁבָּת, כְּאִלּוּ כָּל מְלַאכְתּוֹ עֲשׂוּיָה

**Parallels beyond the library:** **Reshit Chokhmah, Sha'ar HaKedushah 3:5** (Musar) — R. Eliyahu de Vidas cites this Mekhilta as the source for holiness of thought on Shabbat. As Rav Tzadok does with the “other explanation,” he takes it to mean not thinking about worldly matters at all, so the mind can cleave to God.
קְדֻשַּׁת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה מָצִינוּ בְּשַׁבָּת בַּמְּכִילְתָּא

**Parallels beyond the library:** **Reshit Chokhmah, Sha'ar HaYirah 7:19** (Musar/Kabbalah) — the same idea: the soul is the real “person” and the body is only “the flesh of man.” It quotes the Zohar's reading of “You clothed me in skin and flesh.”
וְהַנְּשָׁמָה הִיא הַנִּקְרֵאת אָדָם בַּאֲמִיתּוּת... כִּי הַגּוּף נִקְרָא בְּשַׂר אָדָם
